newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration unveils IRS reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration unveils IRS reform plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Monday unveiled a plan to reform the troubled Internal Revenue Service, long a symbol of a tax system that many feel is unfair and everyone agrees is needlessly complex.
The IRS has been under heavy fire from Congress for mismanaged and failed attempts at updating technology and insensitive treatment of taxpayers.
Critics charge that despite some $4 billion in spending over the past decade, there has been little if any improvement in processing tax returns or in computer and phone answering systems.

The new plan, outlined in a speech by Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, focuses on improving IRS management and seeks a new commissioner skilled in customer service, organisational change and information technolgy.
It comes less than one month before Americans go through the annual ordeal of paying their taxes before the April 15 deadline.
But Summers made clear that making the IRS work better should not be confused with various plans to update or even scrap the U.S. tax system and the IRS along with it.
"The IRS needs to be more responsive to taxpayers, to use technology more effectively and to be more efficient," Summers told a meeting of the Tax Executives Institute.
He said he believed the United States would have an income tax based on the ability of people to pay for the foreseeable future and the IRS would be needed to administer it.
He said the complexity of the tax code and problems at the IRS should not be used to sell extreme measures such as the much-discussed flat tax that he said are complex and unfair in themselves.
"What we must not do is attack the IRS in order to promote other agendas," Summers said.
He told the tax group that the Treasury Department would beef up its oversight of IRS operations, focusing in part, on making private industry expertise more available.
Moreover, he said, the plan gives the IRS itself more flexibility, allowing it to enhance and strengthen its operations without having its hands tied by bureaucratic red tape.
"The IRS faces a multitude of restrictions -- restrictions that would be unacceptable in the private sector -- that hamper its ability to provide efficient service," Summers said.
In addition, Summers said the administration would work with Congress to help the IRS get the stable and predictable funding it needs to operate more effectively.
"Today, the IRS operates in a low-trust, short-tether budgeting environment," he told the meeting. "This makes rational planning for capital projects such as information technology very difficult."
But Summers also made clear that the administration was committed to simplifying the tax code, noting that the president has proposed to exclude up to $500,000 of capital gains on the sale of a home.
This will "dramatically simplify record keeping for more than 60 million families," he said.
